new_statements.quote: [p. 63, sec. 2.4.3] In the Shirongol languages the accent normally falls on the last syllable. This also applies to Eastern Yugur, although predictable deviations occur under some phonetic circumstances (see 3.14.5.). Moghol has final accent as well. The QG languages show vowel reductions in unaccented syllables, and the complete loss of such syllables. This is seen least often in Dongxiang. [p. 35, sec. 1.5.1.1] Word-final accent is shared by all QG languages. This feature is also found in Moghol. [p. 86] In Dagur, the accent falls on the first vowel. In Shirongol it falls on the last vowel, whereas accent placement in Eastern Yugur is more complicated, and partly correlated with vowel length (see 3.14.5.)

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog final stress = final-syllable stress; Nugteren's group-level statements (final accent in all QG languages / in Shirongol, of which Kangjia is a Baoanic member) support exactly that placement. Adds the corollary of unaccented-vowel reduction and lists exceptions only for sister languages (Eastern Yugur, Baoan, Dongxiang), none for Kangjia.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent falls on the last syllable of the stem in all Qinghai-Gansu (QG) Mongolic languages, including the Shirongol group to which Kangjia belongs (Baoanic branch: Baoan, Kangjia, Dongxiang, p. 20); unaccented (non-final) vowels are reduced or lost. The statement is made at the QG/Shirongol group level, not for Kangjia by name; Kangjia-specific indirect support is the reduction of unaccented first-syllable *o > u in Kangjia suqta- < *sogta- 'to get drunk', sunsï- < *sonas- 'to hear' (p. 123).
new_statements.exceptions: For the QG group generally (p. 35): Eastern Yugur has predictable deviations tied to word structure/vowel length and avoidance of ə (3.14.5, p. 174); Baoan compounds carry the main accent on the last syllable of the first member (BaoÑ ˈnudə 'today', taˈwaraŋ '50'); Dongxiang has non-final accent in words whose last vowel became penultimate through epenthesis (ˈbasï 'tiger', ˈbosï 'fabric') and in Arabic and Chinese loanwords (ˈsaχari, ʂïˈʒï 'lion' vs ˈʂïʒï 'persimmon'). No Kangjia-specific exceptions are given. p. 86 adds: 'A less rigid accent placement may also have existed in premodern Shirongol, judging from modern word shapes.' Sec. 1.4.8 'Kangjia phones' (pp. 32-33) describes vowels and consonants only and says nothing about accent.
new_statements.identity_note: Nugteren 2011 treats Kangjia as a member of the Baoanic branch of Shirongol (pp. 13, 20); its Kangjia data are cited after Sečenčogt (1999) (p. 26; Sečenčogt = Siqinchaoketu, the 1999 Kangjia grammar). The accent statements are made for the QG group and for Shirongol as a whole, never for Kangjia by name, so the fixed: final syllable reading for Kangjia is inherited from the group classification plus the Kangjia-specific evidence of unaccented first-syllable *o > u on p. 123. The only Kangjia-specific phonology section (1.4.8, pp. 32-33) is silent on accent.
